title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

errors: Inconsistent first approximation: §12 has x = 4°16'43", y = 4°15'28", so ½(x+y) = 4°16'5.5" and ½(x−y) = 37.5". §14 instead uses ½(x+y) = 4°16'0" and ½(x−y) = 38", i.e. x = 4°16'38", y = 4°15'22". These are rounded or shifted base values, not the stated ones. This is harmless because the base point is only a trial hypothesis.

The claim that the fourth formula is 'spontaneously contained' in the other three is not strictly true. Four equations in three unknowns (x, y, ρ) are overdetermined. The fourth is a consistency condition, satisfied only if the observed times and the adopted radii f, F agree. That is exactly the inconsistency that later surfaces as y > x and is blamed on the shadow size.
Notation for the corrections drifts: p', q' and p'' on this page, but p, q in the text.

Arithmetic checked: a−b, a−b±f, A−B, A−B±F and all their halves are correct. The half-angle reduction of the cosine formula is correct, including sign conventions. The next page's arguments (e.g. 55", 1°0'22", 3°13'0", 4°12'27") follow correctly from hypothesis I.

ideas.what: Determining node longitude and orbital inclination from the four contact times of a total lunar eclipse, via the spherical triangle node–shadow centre–Moon centre
ideas.modern_name: Reduction of lunar eclipse contact timings to orbital elements
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical astronomical practice (18th-century eclipse reductions, e.g. Cassini, Mayer)
ideas.where_published: This posthumous chapter (E838); unsure whether it appears elsewhere in Euler's work

ideas.what: Half-angle (logarithm-friendly) form of the spherical law of cosines: sin²½ρ as a product of two sines over sin u sin v
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard trigonometric identity (well known before Euler)
ideas.where_published: Euler's spherical trigonometry papers (e.g. E214 'Principes de la trigonométrie sphérique')

ideas.what: Solving two nonlinear equations in two unknowns by three trial 'hypotheses' and linear interpolation (regula falsi in two variables), avoiding elimination; also re-parametrizing the trials in sum/difference variables
ideas.modern_name: Multivariable secant / false-position method (precursor of Gauss's hypothesis method and of later secant methods)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Astronomical practice; Gauss (Theoria motus, 1809) for systematic use; modern analysis of multivariable secant methods by Wolfe (1959) and others
ideas.where_published: Euler used trial-and-interpolation methods in orbit computations (e.g. comet work); unsure of an explicit published two-variable regula falsi

ideas.what: Atmospheric enlargement of Earth's shadow inferred as an explanation of eclipse-timing inconsistencies (next page: 1/71 from twilight height, then about 30")
ideas.modern_name: Enlargement of Earth's umbra by the atmosphere
ideas.usually_credited_to: La Hire and others (c. 1700); Mayer's 1/60 rule; modern Chauvet/Danjon conventions
ideas.where_published: Discussed in the following section of E838

deep.surprise_reason: A careful but routine worked example of eclipse reduction using half-angle spherical formulas and a two-variable regula falsi. The numerical method and the shadow-enlargement explanation were both standard practice in the period. Nothing here appears new or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: 'expressionem esse prodituram tam pere complicatam' should read 'prodituram tantopere complicatam' (word split across the line break).
'Proxime vero jam constat esse' – 'esse' is cut off at the right margin in the scan and is a plausible reading.
'y = 4°15'28" − q'' – the trailing '−q' is lost in the margin; it is presumably '−q' parallel to 'x = 4°16'43" − p'.
In §14, 'revera 0'38" − p''' is better read as 0'38" − p and 4°16'0" − q (primes are likely seconds marks or typographic noise).
